reported.text: Two players alternately move one token from node i to some node j>i; a player with no move loses. Given initial token counts, determine the winner under optimal play (a Nim-style analysis).

sources.passage:
Tower Research SDE-1 | 2026 Grad | 85LPA CTC | Please Help 
At Tower Research Capital, a distributed low-latency trading system consists of N sequential processing nodes arranged from left to right.

Each node i initially contains A[i] latency tokens.
A latency token represents pending computational load that can still be forwarded deeper into the pipeline.

Two engineers, Alex and Blake, are stress-testing the routing engine through a turn-based simulation. Alex moves first.

Move Rule

During a turn, a player must:

choose two nodes i and j such that 1 ≤ i < j ≤ N
node i must currently contain at least one latency token

Then the player performs a forward-routing operation:

remove one token from node i
add one token to node j

In other words, one unit of load is pushed strictly forward in the pipeline.

End Condition

A player who cannot make any valid move loses the simulation.

Both players play optimally.

Determine which player wins.

title: Sum of Path MEX-P on Tree

reported.text: MEX-P of a set is the smallest prime that fails to divide some element. For every node u of a tree, compute the sum over all v of MEX-P of the values on the u-v path.

sources.passage:
Tower Research OA | 85LPA CTC | Double Camera On
Tower Research Capital operates a globally distributed low-latency trading infrastructure. Its communication backbone is modeled as a rooted network of interconnected services forming a tree with N servers. Each server processes packets tagged with a positive integer value representing a system property.

To ensure reliable data transmission, Tower Research defines a validation metric called MEX-P on any non-empty set S of positive integers.

MEX-P(S) is defined as the smallest prime number that does not divide at least one element of S.

In other words, among the prime numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, and so on, find the smallest prime p such that there exists at least one value in S that is not divisible by p.

Examples

MEX-P({4, 2, 8, 16}) = 3

All values are divisible by 2, but not all are divisible by 3.

MEX-P({30, 210}) = 7

Both values are divisible by 2, 3, and 5, but 30 is not divisible by 7, so the answer is 7.

The network consists of N servers connected by N − 1 bidirectional communication links, forming a tree. Server i is assigned an integer value Aᵢ.

For any two servers u and v, there exists a unique communication path between them.

Suppose this path consists of the servers:

x₁, x₂, ..., xₖ

where x₁ = u and xₖ = v.

Define

f(u, v) = MEX-P({Aₓ₁, Aₓ₂, ..., Aₓₖ})

That is, compute the MEX-P of all server values appearing on the communication path from u to v.

For every server u, define

Bᵤ = Σ f(u, v) for all 1 ≤ v ≤ N.

In other words, Bᵤ is the sum of the MEX-P values over the communication path between server u and every other server in the network.

Your task is to compute the values:

B₁, B₂, ..., Bₙ.

Input

The first line contains an integer N — the number of servers.
The second line contains N integers A₁, A₂, ..., Aₙ, where Aᵢ is the value assigned to server i.
The next N − 1 lines each contain two integers u and v, representing a bidirectional communication link between servers u and v.

Output

Print N integers:

B₁, B₂, ..., Bₙ,

where Bᵤ is the sum of f(u, v) over all servers v.

title: Max GCD Sum After Root-Path Cut

reported.text: Remove all nodes on the root-to-v path for one chosen v; maximize the sum of GCDs of the remaining components (N up to 2e5).
SDE-1 OA had three very tough problems; one was based on binary (fast) exponentiation.
